claims.claim: The mature mir-204 sequences from all three zebrafish copies are 100% identical.
claims.source: Although each of the three copies of mir-204 in the zebrafish has unique precursor sequences, their mature mir-204 sequences are 100% identical (Figure 2a).
claims.evidence: The manuscript states the identity of mature sequences, with alignment shown in Figure 2a.

claims.claim: Injection of 0.5 ng of pan-204 MO led to highly efficient suppression of mature mir-204 levels.
claims.source: Injection of 0.5 ng of pan-204 MO led to highly efficient suppression of mature mir-204 levels (Figure 2b).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2b.

claims.claim: At the 0.5 ng dose of pan-204 MO there were no noticeable morphological anomalies.
claims.source: At the 0.5 ng dose there were no noticeable morphological anomalies, although slightly higher doses (0.75 ng) resulted in some pericardial edema, jaw defects, mild microcephaly and reduced eye development (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c).
claims.evidence: The manuscript describes observations of morphology at different MO doses, with images shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1c.

claims.claim: Slightly higher doses (0.75 ng) of pan-204 MO resulted in some pericardial edema, jaw defects, mild microcephaly and reduced eye development.
claims.source: At the 0.5 ng dose there were no noticeable morphological anomalies, although slightly higher doses (0.75 ng) resulted in some pericardial edema, jaw defects, mild microcephaly and reduced eye development (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c).
claims.evidence: The manuscript describes observations of morphological defects at 0.75 ng dose, with images shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1c.

claims.claim: Secondary sprouts in mir-204-deficient animals failed to stop at the horizontal myoseptum and form the parachordal line, but instead continued to grow dorsally and contributed to veins.
claims.source: Although initial secondary sprout formation and dorsal growth was normal in mir-204-deficient animals, secondary sprouts in these animals failed to stop at the horizontal myoseptum and form the parachordal line, but instead continued to grow dorsally and contributed to veins (Figure 2d and Figure 2—video 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 2d and Figure 2—video 1.

claims.claim: Pan-204 MO-injected animals formed parachordals in only about 2 segments per 10 somites at three dpf, compared to control animals that had parachordal lines in most somitic segments.
claims.source: Examination of the parachordal line at three dpf (Figure 2e–h,m) showed that compared to control MO-injected animals that had parachordal lines in most somitic segments at this stage (Figure 2e,f,m), pan-204 MO-injected animals formed parachordals in only about 2 segments per 10 somites (Figure 2g,h,m).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging and quantification shown in Figure 2e-h,m.

claims.claim: mir-204-deficient animals displayed nearly complete loss of thoracic duct formation at five dpf.
claims.source: Similarly, examination of the thoracic duct at five dpf (Figure 2i–l,n) showed that control MO-injected animals had a thoracic duct in virtually all segments (Figure 2i,j,n) while mir-204-deficient animals displayed nearly complete loss of thoracic duct formation (Figure 2k,l,n).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging and quantification shown in Figure 2i-l,n.

claims.claim: Injection of 0.5 ng of each individual MO (MO1, MO2, or MO3) alone did not affect lymphatic vessel development.
claims.source: Injection of 0.5 ng of each individual MO alone did not affect lymphatic vessel development (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b–d,i).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging and quantification shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2b-d,i.

claims.claim: Pairwise co-injection of 0.5 ng MO1 and 0.5 ng MO2 resulted in defective thoracic duct formation.
claims.source: Pairwise co-injection of 0.5 ng MO1 and 0.5 ng MO2 resulted in defective thoracic duct formation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2e,j), but pairwise co-injection of either MO1 + MO3 or MO2 + MO3 did not affect lymphatic vessel formation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2f,g,j).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging and quantification shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2e,j.

claims.claim: Pairwise co-injection of either MO1 + MO3 or MO2 + MO3 did not affect lymphatic vessel formation.
claims.source: Pairwise co-injection of 0.5 ng MO1 and 0.5 ng MO2 resulted in defective thoracic duct formation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2e,j), but pairwise co-injection of either MO1 + MO3 or MO2 + MO3 did not affect lymphatic vessel formation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2f,g,j).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging and quantification shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2f,g,j.

claims.claim: Animals injected with 0.5 ng of each of the three MOs (MO1, MO2, and MO3) had lymphatic defects similar to but no more severe than animals injected with either the MO1 + MO2 combination or 0.5 ng of pan-204 MO.
claims.source: Animals injected with 0.5 ng of each of the three MOs (MO1, MO2, and MO3, for a total of 1.5 ng injected) had lymphatic defects similar to but no more severe than animals injected with either the MO1 + MO2 combination or 0.5 ng of pan-204 MO (Figure 2—figure supplement 2h,j and Figure 2n).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging and quantification shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2h,j and Figure 2n.

claims.claim: mir-204-1 and mir-204-2 play relatively more important roles than mir-204-3 during lymphatic development.
claims.source: These results suggest that mir-204–1 and mir-204–2 play relatively more important roles than mir-204–3 during lymphatic development, and confirm that suppressing mir-204 function leads to defective lymphatic vessel formation.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the differential effects of various MO combinations on lymphatic development.

claims.claim: A 22 bp CRISPR/Cas9 mir-204-1 deletion mutant was isolated that deletes the majority of the mature mir-204 sequence (17 out of 22 nt) and the entire seed sequence.
claims.source: Using an active single guide RNA (sgRNA) targeting mir-204–1 (Figure 3a), we isolated a 22 bp CRISPR/Cas9 mir-204–1 deletion mutant that deletes the majority of the mature mir-204 sequence (17 out of 22 nt) and the entire seed sequence at this locus (Figure 3b).
claims.evidence: The manuscript describes the generation and characterization of the mir-204-1 mutant, with sequence alignment shown in Figure 3b.

claims.claim: mir-204-1 homozygous mutants showed only an approximately 20% decrease in mir-204 levels compared to wildtype embryos.
claims.source: Only an approximately 20% decrease in mir-204 levels in mir-204–1 homozygous mutants (miR-204–1-/-) compared to wildtype embryos suggests that reduction from mir-204–1 loss is compensated for by mir-204–2 and/or mir-204–3 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a.

claims.claim: The mir-204-1-/- animals were viable and fertile and did not have obvious morphological defects up to adulthood.
claims.source: The mir-204–1-/- animals were viable and fertile and did not have obvious morphological defects up to adulthood (Figure 3c,d and data not shown).
claims.evidence: The manuscript describes observations of mir-204-1-/- mutant viability and morphology, with images shown in Figure 3c,d.

claims.claim: mir-204-1-/- mutant animals injected with MO2 fail to properly form the thoracic duct and other lymphatic vessels.
claims.source: Entirely consistent with the data generated exclusively using morpholinos (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), mir-204–1-/- mutant animals injected with either MO2 (Figure 3e,h) or with MO2+MO3 (Figure 3g,h) fail to properly form the thoracic duct and other lymphatic vessels, but mir-204–1-/- mutants injected with MO3 developed normal lymphatics (Figure 3f,h).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging and quantification shown in Figure 3e,h.

claims.claim: mir-204-1-/- mutant animals injected with MO2+MO3 fail to properly form the thoracic duct and other lymphatic vessels.
claims.source: Entirely consistent with the data generated exclusively using morpholinos (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), mir-204–1-/- mutant animals injected with either MO2 (Figure 3e,h) or with MO2+MO3 (Figure 3g,h) fail to properly form the thoracic duct and other lymphatic vessels, but mir-204–1-/- mutants injected with MO3 developed normal lymphatics (Figure 3f,h).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging and quantification shown in Figure 3g,h.

claims.claim: mir-204-1-/- mutants injected with MO3 developed normal lymphatics.
claims.source: Entirely consistent with the data generated exclusively using morpholinos (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), mir-204–1-/- mutant animals injected with either MO2 (Figure 3e,h) or with MO2+MO3 (Figure 3g,h) fail to properly form the thoracic duct and other lymphatic vessels, but mir-204–1-/- mutants injected with MO3 developed normal lymphatics (Figure 3f,h).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging and quantification shown in Figure 3f,h.

claims.claim: MO2-injected mir-204-1-/- mutant animals showed defects in parachordal line formation.
claims.source: MO2-injected mir-204–1-/- mutant animals also showed defects in earlier parachordal line formation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b–d), like pan-204 MO-injected animals (Figure 2g,h,m).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging and quantification shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1b-d.

claims.claim: Suppressing biogenesis of mir-204 from the mir-204-1 and mir-204-2 loci is sufficient to disrupt mir-204 function in lymphatic vessel formation.
claims.source: These data indicate that suppressing biogenesis of mir-204 from the mir-204–1 and mir-204–2 loci is sufficient to disrupt mir-204 function in lymphatic vessel formation, regardless of whether a genetic mutant or morpholino is used to suppress miR-204–1.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined results of genetic mutant and morpholino experiments.

claims.claim: mir-204 triple homozygous mutants showed strongly reduced expression of mir-204.
claims.source: Although expression of mir-204 was strongly reduced in mir-204 triple homozygous mutants (Figure 3—figure supplement 2b), they did not display statistically significant lymphatic defects (Figure 3—figure supplement 2c–e), presumably due to an unknown compensatory mechanism taking place in animals where all genomic mature mir-204 sequences are defective.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2b.

claims.claim: mir-204 triple homozygous mutants did not display statistically significant lymphatic defects.
claims.source: Although expression of mir-204 was strongly reduced in mir-204 triple homozygous mutants (Figure 3—figure supplement 2b), they did not display statistically significant lymphatic defects (Figure 3—figure supplement 2c–e), presumably due to an unknown compensatory mechanism taking place in animals where all genomic mature mir-204 sequences are defective.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2c-e.

claims.claim: Embryos injected with mrc1a:mir204-eGFP formed a significantly increased number of thoracic duct segments at three dpf compared to control embryos.
claims.source: In comparison to control embryos that were just beginning thoracic duct formation (Figure 4b), embryos injected with mrc1a:mir204-eGFP formed a significantly increased number of thoracic duct segments (Figure 4c) suggesting that endothelial expression of mir-204 promotes early thoracic duct development (Figure 4d).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging and quantification shown in Figure 4b-d.

claims.claim: Germline transgenic progeny carrying Tg(mrc1a:mir204-egfp) display precocious development of the thoracic duct.
claims.source: Similar to the results from the mosaic analysis, germline transgenic progeny generated from these fish display precocious development of the thoracic duct (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a–c).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging and quantification shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a-c.

claims.claim: Tg(mrc1a:mir204-egfp) animals are viable and fertile with no obvious morphological abnormalities or other defects.
claims.source: These animals are viable and fertile with no obvious morphological abnormalities or other defects, including normal stage-specific spacing between the dorsal aorta and posterior cardinal vein (Figure 4—figure supplement 1d), despite an approximately 2-fold increase in mature miR-204 levels measured by qPCR at three dpf (Figure 4—figure supplement 1e).
claims.evidence: The manuscript describes observations of transgenic animal viability and morphology, with quantification shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1d.

claims.claim: Tg(mrc1a:mir204-egfp) animals have an approximately 2-fold increase in mature miR-204 levels at three dpf.
claims.source: These animals are viable and fertile with no obvious morphological abnormalities or other defects, including normal stage-specific spacing between the dorsal aorta and posterior cardinal vein (Figure 4—figure supplement 1d), despite an approximately 2-fold increase in mature miR-204 levels measured by qPCR at three dpf (Figure 4—figure supplement 1e).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1e.

claims.claim: Increased endothelial mir-204 expression specifically promotes early lymphatic development.
claims.source: These results suggest that increased endothelial mir-204 expression specifically promotes early lymphatic development.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the precocious thoracic duct development observed in transgenic animals overexpressing mir-204.

claims.claim: The loss-of-lymphatic phenotype in MO2-injected mir-204-1-/- embryos was rescued by co-injection of the mrc1a:miR204-eGFP transgene.
claims.source: MO2-injected mir-204–1-/- embryos showed strong suppression of thoracic duct formation (Figure 4e,h,k), but this was rescued by co-injection of the mrc1a:miR204-eGFP transgene (Figure 4f,g,i,j,k), with stronger 'rescue' noted in animals with a higher mosaic contribution from the transgene (Figure 4g,j,k).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging and quantification shown in Figure 4e-k.

claims.claim: Endothelial-autonomous miR-204 function is required for developmental lymphangiogenesis.
claims.source: Together, these data indicate that endothelial-autonomous miR-204 function is required for developmental lymphangiogenesis.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the rescue experiments showing that endothelial-specific mir-204 expression can restore lymphatic development in mir-204-deficient animals.

claims.claim: Human NFATC1 contains a putative miR-204 binding site in its 3'UTR.
claims.source: Human NFATC1 contains a putative miR-204 binding site in its 3'UTR (Figure 5a).
claims.evidence: The manuscript describes the identification of a miR-204 binding site in the NFATC1 3'UTR, with sequence alignment shown in Figure 5a.

claims.claim: Luciferase reporter activity containing the NFATC1 3'UTR was significantly suppressed in the presence of miR-204 but not in the presence of miR-126 control.
claims.source: Luciferase reporter activity was significantly suppressed in the presence of miR-204 but not in the presence of the miR-126 control (Figure 5b).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 5b.

claims.claim: Mutating four nucleotides in the seed binding sequence of the NFATC1 3'UTR rendered the construct insensitive to suppression by miR-204.
claims.source: To confirm the specificity of NFATC1 miR-204 target site recognition, we mutated four nucleotides in the seed binding sequence of the NFATC1 3'UTR (Figure 5a) and demonstrated that this rendered the construct insensitive to suppression by miR-204 (Figure 5b), confirming that this binding site is critical for direct targeting.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by luciferase reporter assay data with mutated constructs shown in Figure 5b.

claims.claim: Overexpression of miR-204 in human LECs suppressed endogenous NFATC1 expression.
claims.source: Overexpression of miR-204 in human LECs suppressed endogenous NFATC1 expression while miR-204 inhibitor (antagomir) increased endogenous NFATC1 expression, showing that miR-204 also regulates endogenous NFATC1 transcript levels in human LEC (Figure 5c).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5c.

claims.claim: miR-204 inhibitor (antagomir) increased endogenous NFATC1 expression in human LECs.
claims.source: Overexpression of miR-204 in human LECs suppressed endogenous NFATC1 expression while miR-204 inhibitor (antagomir) increased endogenous NFATC1 expression, showing that miR-204 also regulates endogenous NFATC1 transcript levels in human LEC (Figure 5c).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5c.

claims.claim: Zebrafish nfatc1 contains a mir-204 binding site in its 3'UTR.
claims.source: Zebrafish nfatc1 also contains a mir-204 binding site in its 3'UTR (Figure 5d).
claims.evidence: The manuscript describes the identification of a mir-204 binding site in the zebrafish nfatc1 3'UTR, with sequence alignment shown in Figure 5d.

claims.claim: The activity of a luciferase reporter containing the zebrafish nfatc1 3'UTR is strongly suppressed by miR-204.
claims.source: The activity of a luciferase reporter containing the zebrafish nfatc1 3'UTR is also strongly suppressed by miR-204, and this suppression is fully rescued by mutating the seed binding sequence in the nfatc1 3'UTR (Figure 5e).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 5e.

claims.claim: Suppression of miR-204 by mutating the seed binding sequence in the zebrafish nfatc1 3'UTR fully rescued the suppression by miR-204.
claims.source: The activity of a luciferase reporter containing the zebrafish nfatc1 3'UTR is also strongly suppressed by miR-204, and this suppression is fully rescued by mutating the seed binding sequence in the nfatc1 3'UTR (Figure 5e).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by luciferase reporter assay data with mutated constructs shown in Figure 5e.

claims.claim: mir-204 knockdown using the pan-204 MO results in increased levels of endogenous nfatc1 transcript in five dpf zebrafish embryos.
claims.source: Importantly, mir-204 knockdown using the pan-204 MO (targeting all three zebrafish mir-204s) results in increased levels of endogenous nfatc1 transcript in five dpf zebrafish embryos (Figure 5f).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5f.

claims.claim: miR-204-mediated regulation of NFATC1 is conserved between human and zebrafish.
claims.source: Together, these data demonstrate conserved miR-204-mediated regulation of NFATC1.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the luciferase and qPCR data showing miR-204 regulation of NFATC1 in both human and zebrafish.

claims.claim: Loss of Nfatc1 in mice is associated with lymphatic hyperplasia.
claims.source: As noted above, loss of Nfatc1 in mice is associated with lymphatic hyperplasia (Norrmén et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on a citation to previous work by Norrmén et al., 2009.

claims.claim: Knockdown of nfatc1 in zebrafish using two different morpholinos causes thoracic duct enlargement.
claims.source: Using two different morpholinos targeting nfatc1 (splice MO and ATG MO), we show that knockdown of this gene in the zebrafish also causes thoracic duct enlargement, similar to that shown in mice, with no noticeable abnormal blood vessel formation (Figure 6a–e and Figure 6—figure supplement 1a–e).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging and quantification shown in Figure 6a-e and Figure 6—figure supplement 1a-e.

claims.claim: Zebrafish larvae treated with a low dose of CsA (1 ug/mL) displayed thoracic duct enlargement phenotype observed in nfatc1 MO-injected animals.
claims.source: The zebrafish larvae treated with a low doses of CsA (1 ug/mL) also displayed thoracic duct enlargement phenotype observed in nfatc1 MO-injected animals (Figure 6—figure supplement 1f–j).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging and quantification shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1f-j.

claims.claim: nfatc1△8/△8 mutants had enlarged thoracic ducts at five dpf.
claims.source: Like nfatc1 morphants and CsA-treated animals, nfatc1△8/△8 mutants also had enlarged thoracic ducts at five dpf (Figure 6g–k).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging and quantification shown in Figure 6g-k.

claims.claim: nfatc1 is required for proper lymphatic development in the zebrafish.
claims.source: Therefore, consistent with previous data in mice, our results suggest that nfatc1 is required for proper lymphatic development in the zebrafish.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the lymphatic defects observed in nfatc1 morphants, CsA-treated animals, and nfatc1 mutants.

claims.claim: In animals co-injected with both pan-204 MO and nfatc1 splice MO, formation of the thoracic duct is largely restored.
claims.source: However, in animals co-injected with both pan-204 MO and nfatc1 splice MO, formation of the thoracic duct is largely restored (Figure 7c,f,j), as is the formation other lymphatic vessels including the DLLV and intersegmental lymphatics (ISLV) (Figure 7c,i,k).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging and quantification shown in Figure 7c,f,j.

claims.claim: In animals co-injected with both pan-204 MO and nfatc1 splice MO, formation of the DLLV and intersegmental lymphatics is restored.
claims.source: However, in animals co-injected with both pan-204 MO and nfatc1 splice MO, formation of the thoracic duct is largely restored (Figure 7c,f,j), as is the formation other lymphatic vessels including the DLLV and intersegmental lymphatics (ISLV) (Figure 7c,i,k).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging and quantification shown in Figure 7c,i,k.

claims.claim: Abnormal lymphatic vessel development in mir-204 deficient animals can be substantially rescued by suppressing nfatc1 expression.
claims.source: These results suggest that abnormal lymphatic vessel development in mir-204 deficient animals can be substantially rescued by suppressing nfatc1 expression.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the rescue experiments showing that nfatc1 knockdown restores lymphatic development in mir-204-deficient animals.

claims.claim: A proper balance between mir-204 and nfatc1 is critical for proper lymphatic vessel development.
claims.source: Based on all of our findings, we propose that a proper balance between mir-204 and nfatc1 is critical for proper lymphatic vessel development, with loss of either mir-204 or nfatc1 causing defects in lymphatic vessel formation (Figure 7l).
claims.evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from all the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Loss of either mir-204 or nfatc1 causes defects in lymphatic vessel formation.
claims.source: Based on all of our findings, we propose that a proper balance between mir-204 and nfatc1 is critical for proper lymphatic vessel development, with loss of either mir-204 or nfatc1 causing defects in lymphatic vessel formation (Figure 7l).
claims.evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from all the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: The lymphatic system is important for fluid and protein homeostasis, lipid transport, and immunity.
claims.source: The lymphatic system is important for fluid and protein homeostasis, lipid transport, and immunity.
claims.evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about the lymphatic system.

claims.claim: Lymphatic malfunction is linked to many pathologies including lymphedema, cancer metastasis, and cardiovascular disease.
claims.source: Lymphatic malfunction is linked to many pathologies including lymphedema, cancer metastasis, and cardiovascular disease (Petrova and Koh, 2018; Venero Galanternik et al., 2016; Alitalo, 2011; Stacker et al., 2014; Lim et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Primitive lymphatic vessels are derived from lymphatic endothelial cell (LEC) progenitors that transdifferentiate from venous blood endothelial cells (BECs) and subsequently migrate away from the veins to form lymphatic vessels.
claims.source: Primitive lymphatic vessels are derived from lymphatic endothelial cell (LEC) progenitors that transdifferentiate from venous blood endothelial cells (BECs) and subsequently migrate away from the veins to form lymphatic vessels (Sabin, 1902; Hong et al., 2002; Koltowska et al., 2013; Nicenboim et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claims.claim: PROX1, SOX18, COUPTFII, VEGFC/VEGFR3, NRP2, CCBE1, CLEC2, YAP/TAZ, and NFATC1 are required for proper regulation of lymphangiogenesis during development and disease.
claims.source: A variety of factors have been identified that are required for proper regulation of lymphangiogenesis during development and disease, including PROX1, SOX18, COUPTFII, VEGFC/VEGFR3, NRP2, CCBE1, CLEC2, YAP/TAZ, and NFATC1 (Wigle and Oliver, 1999; Dumont et al., 1998; Karkkainen et al., 2004; François et al., 2008; Srinivasan et al., 2010; Yuan et al., 2002; Uhrin et al., 2010; Hogan et al., 2009; Kulkarni et al., 2009; Sweet et al., 2015; Bui et al., 2016; Cho et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claims.claim: The development of the zebrafish lymphatic vascular system is highly conserved and stereotyped.
claims.source: The development of the zebrafish lymphatic vascular system is highly conserved and stereotyped (Yaniv et al., 2006; Okuda et al., 2012; Jung et al., 2017; Küchler et al., 2006), and the availability of transgenic zebrafish expressing fluorescent reporters in lymphatic endothelium makes it straightforward to monitor lymphatic development at the single cell level in vivo and visualize even subtle lymphatic defects using optimized high-resolution microscopy technologies (Jung et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claims.claim: MicroRNAs are important posttranscriptional regulators that play crucial roles in developmental, physiological, and disease-related processes in animals.
claims.source: MicroRNAs are important posttranscriptional regulators that play crucial roles in developmental, physiological, and disease-related processes in animals (Gebert and MacRae, 2019).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: MicroRNAs are noncoding RNAs approximately 22 nucleotide long that guide Argonaute proteins for gene silencing by mRNA degradation and/or translational repression.
claims.source: They are noncoding RNAs approximately 22 nucleotide long that guide Argonaute proteins for gene silencing by mRNA degradation and/or translational repression (Jonas and Izaurralde, 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Targeting of microRNAs is accomplished by binding of the key nucleotides 2-8 (the 'seed' sequence) and additional microRNA sequences to complementary sequences in target mRNAs.
claims.source: Targeting of microRNAs is accomplished by binding of the key nucleotides 2–8 (the 'seed' sequence) and additional microRNA sequences to complementary sequences in target mRNAs (Bartel, 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: The majority of microRNA target sites are located in the 3' untranslated regions (UTRs) of mRNAs.
claims.source: The majority of microRNA target sites are located in the 3' untranslated regions (UTRs) of mRNAs, although some microRNA targeting also occurs in 5'UTR and coding sequences (Tay et al., 2008; Lytle et al., 2007; Jung et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Some microRNA targeting occurs in 5'UTR and coding sequences.
claims.source: The majority of microRNA target sites are located in the 3' untranslated regions (UTRs) of mRNAs, although some microRNA targeting also occurs in 5'UTR and coding sequences (Tay et al., 2008; Lytle et al., 2007; Jung et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: MicroRNA regulatory networks are thought to confer robustness to biological processes by reinforcing transcription programs and attenuating aberrant transcripts.
claims.source: MicroRNA regulatory networks are thought to confer robustness to biological processes by reinforcing transcription programs and attenuating aberrant transcripts by either switching off or fine-tuning gene expression, helping to buffer against random fluctuations in transcript copy number (Ebert and Sharp, 2012; Staton et al., 2011; Choi et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: BEC-specific microRNAs such as miR-31 and miR-181a target Prox1 and prevent lymphatic specification in BECs.
claims.source: Profiling of microRNAs in human lymphatic endothelial cells (LECs) and blood endothelial cells (BECs) has identified BEC-specific microRNAs such as miR-31 and miR-181a that target Prox1 and prevent lymphatic specification in BECs (Leslie Pedrioli et al., 2010; Kazenwadel et al., 2010; Dunworth et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Some microRNAs can help BECs retain their identity by negatively regulating lymphatic development.
claims.source: These studies suggest some microRNAs can help BECs retain their identity by negatively regulating lymphatic development.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the studies showing BEC-specific microRNAs target lymphatic genes.

claims.claim: Manipulation of endothelial microRNAs has been shown to result in defective lymphatic development.
claims.source: Manipulation of endothelial microRNAs has also been shown to result in defective lymphatic development (Kontarakis et al., 2018; Nicoli et al., 2012; Chen et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: The majority of the 30 highly significantly LEC-enriched microRNAs identified were specific to mammals.
claims.source: The majority of the 30 highly significantly LEC-enriched microRNAs we identified were specific to mammals, with only seven microRNAs conserved in other vertebrate species.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on analysis of the sequencing data and conservation of the identified microRNAs.

claims.claim: Only seven of the 30 highly significantly LEC-enriched microRNAs are conserved in other vertebrate species.
claims.source: The majority of the 30 highly significantly LEC-enriched microRNAs we identified were specific to mammals, with only seven microRNAs conserved in other vertebrate species.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on analysis of the sequencing data and conservation of the identified microRNAs.

claims.claim: Most LEC microRNAs have diverged and/or evolved for mammalian-specific functions.
claims.source: This suggests that most of these LEC microRNAs have diverged and/or evolved for mammalian-specific functions.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that most LEC-enriched microRNAs are mammal-specific.

claims.claim: miR-204 plays an important conserved role during lymphatic development.
claims.source: The most highly LEC-enriched microRNA was miR-204, a microRNA with 100% sequence identity across a broad swath of vertebrate species (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a), suggesting it plays an important conserved role during lymphatic development.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the high conservation of miR-204 sequence across vertebrates.

claims.claim: The study also uncovered microRNAs such as miR-326, miR-139, miR-338, miR-148a, and miR-30d that had been previously reported to be LEC-enriched.
claims.source: In addition to miR-204 and a number of other newly identified LEC-enriched microRNAs, we also uncovered microRNAs such as miR-326, miR-139, miR-338, miR-148a, and miR-30d that had been previously reported to be LEC-enriched (Leslie Pedrioli et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on comparison with previous studies, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: miR-204 was not identified in the previous study by Pedrioli et al, despite its being the most highly enriched lymphatic microRNA in the current study.
claims.source: Intriguingly, miR-204 was not identified in the previous study by Pedrioli et al, despite its being the most highly enriched lymphatic microRNA in our study, while the most enriched LEC microRNA reported by Pedrioli et al, miR-95, was excluded from our analysis due to a low number of sequence reads.

results.result: Small RNA sequencing of human lymphatic (HMVEC-dLy) and blood (HUVEC) endothelial cells identified miR-204-5p as the most highly enriched microRNA in lymphatic endothelial cells, with 105-fold higher representation compared to blood endothelial cells, validated by qPCR.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C11 provide comprehensive experimental evidence including appropriate biological replicates (n=3), validated cell types expressing appropriate markers (C2-C3), stringent filtering criteria (C5), statistical significance (p<0.01, FDR<0.01, C6), and independent qPCR validation (C10). The methodology is sound and the conclusion is well-supported by converging lines of evidence.

results.result: Zebrafish mir-204 is highly enriched in FACS-sorted lymphatic endothelial cells compared to arterial and venous blood endothelial cells, demonstrating evolutionary conservation of lymphatic-specific mir-204 expression between humans and zebrafish.
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C14 demonstrate conservation of mir-204 enrichment in lymphatic cells across species using FACS-sorted zebrafish endothelial populations with appropriate transgenic markers. The qPCR data (C12-C13) and comparative analysis (C14) provide strong evidence for evolutionary conservation, though the claim would be strengthened by reporting the number of biological replicates for the zebrafish experiments.

results.result: miR-204 is located in intronic regions of TRPM genes and shows 100% sequence conservation across vertebrate species, with zebrafish having three paralogous copies (mir-204-1, mir-204-2, mir-204-3) that produce identical mature sequences.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C20 describe the genomic organization and conservation of mir-204, supported by sequence alignments and database citations. The 100% conservation of mature sequence (C16, C20) and genomic locations (C15, C18-C19) are well-documented. However, these are primarily descriptive/bioinformatic findings rather than novel experimental discoveries.

results.result: Morpholino-mediated knockdown of mir-204 using pan-204 MO (0.5 ng dose) causes severe lymphatic defects in zebrafish, including failure of secondary sprouts to form parachordal lines and nearly complete loss of thoracic duct formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C26 demonstrate robust loss-of-function phenotypes with appropriate dose optimization (C21-C23), time-lapse imaging (C24), and quantitative analysis at multiple developmental stages (C25-C26). Sample sizes are adequate (n=23-39) and statistical significance is demonstrated. The phenotype is severe and reproducible, supporting a critical role for mir-204 in lymphatic development.

results.result: Individual morpholinos targeting each of the three zebrafish mir-204 paralogs show that mir-204-1 and mir-204-2 play more important roles than mir-204-3 during lymphatic development, with combined MO1+MO2 knockdown sufficient to cause lymphatic defects.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C31 systematically dissect the relative contributions of the three mir-204 paralogs using individual and combinatorial morpholino injections. The experimental design is logical and the results clearly demonstrate differential importance of the paralogs (C28-C30). However, the conclusion (C31) is appropriately stated as a suggestion rather than definitive proof, as functional redundancy and compensation mechanisms may complicate interpretation.

results.result: A CRISPR/Cas9-generated mir-204-1 deletion mutant combined with morpholino knockdown of mir-204-2 recapitulates the lymphatic defects seen with pan-204 morpholino, confirming that suppressing mir-204-1 and mir-204-2 is sufficient to disrupt lymphatic vessel formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C39 provide genetic validation of the morpholino results using CRISPR/Cas9 mutagenesis. The mutant characterization is thorough (C32-C34), and the combinatorial genetic/morpholino approach (C35-C37) elegantly confirms the morpholino findings while avoiding potential off-target effects. The consistency between genetic and morpholino approaches (C39) strongly supports the conclusions. Sample sizes are adequate and quantification is provided.

results.result: Triple homozygous mutants lacking all three mir-204 paralogs show strongly reduced mir-204 expression but do not display statistically significant lymphatic defects, suggesting compensatory mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C41 present a puzzling result that contradicts the morpholino and genetic+morpholino findings. While the qPCR data (C40) confirms reduced mir-204 levels, the lack of phenotype (C41) is unexplained. The authors speculate about compensation but provide no mechanistic insight or additional experiments to test this hypothesis. This result raises questions about the interpretation of the morpholino experiments and requires further investigation.

results.result: Endothelial-specific overexpression of mir-204 using the mrc1a promoter causes precocious thoracic duct development at 3 dpf in both mosaic and germline transgenic animals, with transgenic animals showing approximately 2-fold increased mir-204 levels and no morphological abnormalities.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C46 demonstrate gain-of-function effects complementing the loss-of-function studies. The use of both mosaic (C42) and germline transgenic approaches (C43-C45) strengthens the findings. Quantification shows significant acceleration of lymphatic development (C42-C43) without gross morphological defects (C44), and the modest 2-fold increase in mir-204 levels (C45) is physiologically relevant. The conclusion (C46) is appropriately stated as a suggestion.

results.result: Endothelial-specific expression of mir-204 rescues lymphatic development in mir-204-1-/- mutants injected with MO2, demonstrating that endothelial-autonomous miR-204 function is required for developmental lymphangiogenesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C48 provide critical rescue experiments demonstrating cell-autonomous function. The experimental design is rigorous, using genetic mutants combined with morpholinos to eliminate mir-204 function, then rescuing with endothelial-specific transgene expression. The dose-dependent rescue (C47) and quantification strengthen the conclusion. This is a key result establishing the cell-autonomous requirement for mir-204 in lymphatic endothelium.

results.result: Human NFATC1 is a direct target of miR-204, as demonstrated by luciferase reporter assays showing miR-204-dependent suppression that is abolished by seed sequence mutation, and by miR-204 mimic/inhibitor experiments showing reciprocal regulation of endogenous NFATC1 in human lymphatic endothelial cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C53 provide multiple lines of evidence for direct targeting: bioinformatic prediction (C49), luciferase reporter assays with wild-type and mutant constructs (C50-C51), and regulation of endogenous NFATC1 by miR-204 mimic and inhibitor (C52-C53). The experimental design is rigorous, including appropriate controls (miR-126) and seed sequence mutations. Four biological replicates were used for luciferase assays. This establishes NFATC1 as a bona fide miR-204 target.

results.result: Zebrafish nfatc1 is also a direct target of mir-204, demonstrated by conserved binding sites, luciferase reporter assays, and increased endogenous nfatc1 expression upon mir-204 knockdown, establishing evolutionary conservation of miR-204/NFATC1 regulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C58 demonstrate conservation of the miR-204/NFATC1 regulatory relationship in zebrafish using parallel approaches to the human studies. The luciferase assays (C55-C56) and in vivo validation (C57) are well-controlled. The conclusion of evolutionary conservation (C58) is well-supported by the combined human and zebrafish data. This strengthens the biological significance of the miR-204/NFATC1 axis.

results.result: Loss of nfatc1 function in zebrafish, achieved through morpholino knockdown, pharmacological inhibition with cyclosporin A, or CRISPR/Cas9 mutagenesis, causes thoracic duct enlargement/lymphatic hyperplasia similar to mouse Nfatc1 mutants.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C63 establish the zebrafish nfatc1 phenotype using three independent approaches: two different morpholinos (C60), pharmacological inhibition (C61), and genetic mutation (C62). The consistency across methods and with published mouse data (C59) strongly supports the conclusion (C63). Sample sizes are adequate (n=8-10) and quantification is provided. This validates zebrafish as a model for studying NFATC1 function in lymphatic development.

results.result: Co-injection of nfatc1 morpholino with pan-204 morpholino substantially rescues lymphatic vessel formation in mir-204-deficient animals, demonstrating that balanced expression of mir-204 and nfatc1 is critical for proper lymphatic development.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C66 provide the critical genetic interaction experiment demonstrating that nfatc1 is a functionally relevant target of mir-204 in vivo. The rescue of both thoracic duct (C64) and other lymphatic vessels (C65) by nfatc1 knockdown in mir-204-deficient animals is compelling evidence for the miR-204/NFATC1 regulatory axis. The conclusions (C67-C68) are well-supported by the combined loss-of-function, gain-of-function, and rescue experiments. Sample sizes are adequate (n=8-21).

results.result: Background information establishing the importance of the lymphatic system, the developmental origin of lymphatic vessels, known regulators of lymphangiogenesis, the zebrafish model system, and the role of microRNAs in gene regulation and vascular development.

The claims accurately represent the current state of knowledge in the field and provide necessary context for interpreting the experimental results.

The observation that most LEC-enriched microRNAs are mammal-specific (C83-C84) while miR-204 is highly conserved (C86) provides rationale for focusing on miR-204.
